title: Conditional Statements
description: if/else chains, nested conditionals, and both traditional and modern switch statements.
objectives: Write if/else if/else chains and nested conditionals
Write and correctly terminate switch statements
Understand modern switch expressions at a conceptual level

content.heading: if / else if / else
content.body: Java's conditional structure mirrors C's: if (condition) { ... } else if (condition) { ... } else { ... }, where condition must be a boolean expression (unlike C, Java does not accept an int as a condition). Only the first matching branch runs. Braces are technically optional for single-statement bodies, but omitting them is a common source of subtle bugs when code is later modified without adding braces back — most style guides recommend always using them.

content.heading: switch Statements
content.body:
A traditional switch (expression) { case value1: ...; break; case value2: ...; break; default: ...; } compares expression against each case label. Crucially, without a break statement at the end of each case's code, execution falls through into the next case regardless of its label — a frequent source of bugs for those coming from languages without this behavior. default handles any value not matched by an explicit case. switch works with byte/short/char/int (and their wrapper types), String (since Java 7), and enum types.

Since Java 14, a modern switch expression form is available: switch (x) { case 1 -> doA(); case 2 -> doB(); default -> doC(); }, using -> instead of : and break, which does not fall through by default and can also be used as an expression that produces a value directly. Both forms coexist in modern Java; the classic colon-and-break form remains extremely common in existing code.

content.explanation: The classic switch requires break to avoid falling through into the next case. The modern switch expression form assigns dayName directly and needs no break, since -> cases don't fall through.

keyPoints: Java conditions must be boolean expressions — no implicit int-to-boolean conversion
Classic switch falls through to the next case without an explicit break
switch works with primitives (excluding long/float/double/boolean), String, and enums
Modern switch expressions (Java 14+, using ->) don't fall through and can produce a value directly
commonMistakes: Forgetting break in a classic switch, causing unintended fall-through
Omitting braces on a single-statement if body and later adding a second statement, unintentionally excluding it from the condition
Trying to switch on a long, float, double, or boolean, none of which switch supports
